question: How do candles, lamps and soap become industries — and what replaces slaves with palm oil on the African coast?
thesis: Between 1750 and 1850 fat becomes a chemical, industrial and imperial matter. Whale oil and spermaceti reach their peak and spread to every ocean; West African palm oil takes the place of the slave trade in Liverpool and Bristol and greases the machines; soap consumption doubles under the new chemistry of fats; and light moves from the oil lamp to gas.

big_ideas.title: Whaling peaks and goes round the world
big_ideas.text: Spermaceti gives the brightest candle, the American fleet reaches 735 ships, and as the Dutch fishery collapses the hunt spreads to Walvis Bay, the Derwent, Cook Strait and Honolulu. Whale oil is a global industry, and it runs on shore stations and ports as much as on ships.

big_ideas.title: Palm oil replaces the slave trade, but not slavery
big_ideas.text: After Britain abolishes the slave trade in 1807 the Bight of Biafra ports and Liverpool’s slave-trading houses turn to palm oil, and British imports rise tenfold in a generation. The oil is made from tended groves, not plantations, and Law argues that the demand for soap increases slavery inside West Africa.

big_ideas.title: Chemistry and machines make soap and light industrial
big_ideas.text: Chevreul shows what a fat is, Leblanc soda and steam power remake soap making, soap consumption more than doubles, and the Marseille kettles of olive oil face imported seed oils. At the same time the Argand lamp and gaslight change what a lamp burns.

big_ideas.title: Small fats with large futures
big_ideas.text: Cod liver oil is a medicine before vitamins, the Russian sunflower escapes the Lenten list of forbidden oils, Franciscans plant olives in California, and a Malayan superintendent plants coconuts: four fats on the margins that will matter later.

threads.title: Whaling: peak and spread
threads.claim: American and other fleets take over from the Dutch, and shore stations and island ports carry the hunt to the southern oceans.

beats.text: Colonists learn to make spermaceti candles, and a Trust of 1761 tries to control the oil.
With the Revolution having cut Britain off from New England oil, twenty to thirty Yankee whaleships work Walvis Bay.
The revolutionary wars end the Dutch whale fishery, which had sent 178 ships to Spitsbergen in 1670.
Whaling is Tasmania’s first industry, with right whales so thick in the Derwent that fifty or sixty can be seen at once.
American whaling grows from 25 ships at Nantucket in 1815 to a fleet of 735.
Honolulu and Lahaina become the whalers’ Pacific ports, with six hundred arrivals in 1846.
New Zealand has perhaps a hundred shore whaling stations, most on Cook Strait.

threads.title: West African palm oil
threads.claim: A trade built by slave-trading ports and houses turns into the supply of Britain’s soap, candles and machine grease.

beats.text: Britain abolishes the slave trade, and the Bight of Biafra ports turn to palm oil, though Law warns ‘legitimate commerce’ is a Eurocentric label.
Liverpool slave-trading houses become palm-oil importers, among them Horsfall, founder of the city’s largest palm-oil firm.
Old Calabar and then Bonny lead the oil export, and in 1855 the Bight’s ports ship 25,060 tons.
British palm-oil imports rise from under 2,000 tons a year to over 22,000.
Law argues that Britain’s soap boom drives the use of slave labour inside West Africa.
Palm oil lubricates railways and machinery and is a base for soap, candles and glycerine.
The oil is made from natural groves of 200 to 300 palms to the hectare, tended by local farmers.
Bristol, a soap-making city, becomes a palm-oil port.

threads.title: Soap and light become industrial
threads.claim: Taxed soap can be counted, and chemistry and machinery change how it and its light are made.

beats.text: Britain’s soap excise leaves a record: consumption rises from 3.1 pounds a head in 1791 to 8 pounds in the 1860s.
Argand’s lamp with a tubular wick and glass chimney burns oil without smoke.
British soap consumption more than doubles, from 3.1 to 8 pounds a head.
Steam power, Leblanc soda and Chevreul’s chemistry make soap making industrial.
Marseille’s olive-oil soap meets imported oilseeds in its kettles.
Gaslight, ‘a light without a wick’, is put before a Commons committee.
Chevreul shows that fats are compounds of fatty acids and glycerine and explains saponification.

threads.title: Small fats with large futures
threads.claim: Four fats that stay marginal in this period become important in the next.

beats.text: Cod liver oil is used as a medicine, and the hunt begins for its active principle.
Serra plants olives at San Diego, and Jefferson admires the trees.
In Russia the sunflower is not on the Lenten list of forbidden oils, and the seed is taken up eagerly.
James Low’s coconut and nutmeg estates at Province Wellesley, worked partly by convicts from India.

turning_points.text: Spermaceti candles become the foundation of colonial whaling.
Franciscans plant olives at San Diego.
Argand’s lamp burns oil without smoke.
Yankee whalers reach Walvis Bay as Dutch whaling ends.
Britain abolishes the slave trade and the oil trade fills its place.
Chevreul begins the chemistry of fats.
American whaling enters its golden age.
Honolulu becomes the Pacific whalers’ port.
Soap demand drives slavery inside West Africa.
Britain’s soap excise, which let consumption be counted, ends.

text: Fifteen entries around Britain, Paris, Marseille and Russia: soap excise and abolition, Chevreul, Argand and gas, Liverpool and Bristol houses, palm oil in Britain, the Dutch whale fishery’s collapse, the Russian sunflower’s Lenten loophole and cod liver oil as a medicine ([[o2]], [[o1]], [[th1]], [[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec4]], [[ec8]], [[ec3]], [[w1]], [[b1]], [[th2]]).
No entry. Nothing in the library covers the Ottoman and Egyptian fats of these years.

One entry: the coconut and nutmeg estates of James Low at Province Wellesley, worked partly by convicts from India ([[ec13]]). Indian, Chinese and Japanese oilseed and whale traditions are otherwise missing from this folio.

The Bight of Biafra becomes the world’s oil coast: the groves, the ports, slavery inside Africa, and Walvis Bay ([[x1]], [[x3]], [[l1]], [[ec11]]); and, inland, Cameroon’s Grassfields chiefdoms run their own palm-oil tribute economy, raiding their lowland producers for oil and rationing the iron they traded back ([[ec14]]). Law, Lynn and Hopkins supply the Atlantic-coast economic history; Rowlands and Warnier’s Grassfields entry is the one place African producers appear on their own terms rather than as an export statistic.
Spermaceti candles, Nantucket’s fleet and Franciscan olive trees ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[x2]]).

Three entries from Ellis and Dolin: Tasmania’s Derwent and New Zealand’s Cook Strait stations, where Maori served as ‘toungers’, and the Hawaiian ports where the Pacific fleet stopped ([[ec9]], [[ec10]], [[ec12]]). These are whaling economies run by Europeans and Americans; nothing in the library records Pacific fats from an islander’s side.

sources.intro: Dolin and Davis et al. for American whaling; Schivelbusch for light; Ward and Lowengard for soap and chemistry; Law, Lynn, Hopkins and Kiple for palm oil.
main: Dolin and Davis, Gallman & Gleiter ([[ec1]], [[ec2]]); Ellis ([[w1]]).
Law, Lynn, Hopkins and Kiple for palm oil ([[o1]], [[ec3]], [[x1]], [[x3]], [[ec4]], [[ec8]], [[ec7]], [[l1]]); Mueller and Kiple for the olive ([[x2]]).
Ellis for the Tasmanian, New Zealand and Namibian whale coasts ([[ec9]], [[ec10]], [[ec11]]).
Dolin for the Hawaiian ports ([[ec12]]); Lees for Penang’s estates ([[ec13]]).
Kiple (Heiser) for the Russian sunflower ([[b1]]); Kiple (O’Keefe) for cod liver oil ([[th2]]).
contested: Dolin gives the fleet's peak as both 1846 and 1854 ([[ec2]]).
Law's argument that the oil boom increased slavery in Africa is a thesis ([[l1]]).
Ward does not name the imported oils that challenged the olive ([[ec5]]).

The Lenten sunflower story is Heiser’s, from Gilmore (1931), with ‘perhaps unknown to the church authorities’ his guess ([[b1]]); cod liver oil’s eighteenth-century medical use is ‘reportedly’ so ([[th2]]).
gaps: Tallow imports from Russia, rapeseed and colza lamp oil, and Marseille’s own records were not read.

India, China and Japan are absent from this folio, and so is the Near East; Oceania appears only as a whale coast, with no Maori or Pacific Islander producer’s voice beyond Ellis’s mention of ‘toungers’.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.
*Economy* has the quantities; *Technology* the lamp, gas and the soap chemistry; *Order* and *Lives* the abolition and its limits.
The Nexus connects the industrial soap chain to the palm-oil boom.

The *picture by region* counts the 26 entries: Europe 15, Far East 1, Africa 4, Americas 3, Oceania 3; none in Near East or Worldwide. It is a British-led story with two edges: African producers and southern-hemisphere whale coasts.
